title: Collection expression arguments and extension indexers
body: C# 15 ships with .NET 11, whose release candidates carry a go-live licence; general availability is expected in November 2026. These examples are checked with SDK 11.0.100-rc.2. Details can still change before release, so re-check the What's new page after GA.

Collection expressions (stage 6) could not pass constructor arguments, so specifying a capacity or a comparer meant falling back to `new`. C# 15 allows a `with(...)` element first: `List<string> names = [with(capacity: 32), ..source];` or `HashSet<string> set = [with(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), "a", "A"];`. The arguments go to the collection's constructor or factory method.

This matters for correctness, not just speed: a dictionary or set built with the wrong comparer behaves differently. `Dictionary<string, int> d = [with(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), ...]` keeps the concise syntax while stating the equality rule.

C# 15 also allows indexers in extension blocks (stage 13): `extension(IEnumerable<int> sequence) { public int this[int index] => sequence.ElementAt(index); }` lets callers write `numbers[2]` on a type that has no indexer. An extension block that declares an indexer must name its receiver.

Extension indexers are resolved statically like other extensions, and an instance indexer on the type always wins: an extension indexer on `string` is never chosen for `text[1]`, because `string` already has one. Check the cost hidden behind the brackets: indexing an `IEnumerable<T>` by position is O(n), unlike an array or list.
challenge: Create a SortedSet<string> with a descending comparer using a collection expression argument, add apple, cherry and banana, and print the set in order.
question: In `HashSet<string> s = [with(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), "a", "A"];`, what does with(...) do?
correct: Passes the comparer to the HashSet constructor before the elements are added
wrong: Adds the comparer as an element
Applies the comparer only when printing
reasoning: with(...) must come first and supplies constructor or factory arguments, so the set holds one element.
